lignes.texte: “You’re too young for cancer.”
That single sentence is killing thousands of 20 to 30 year olds.
When a healthy 28 year old sits on an examination table with rectal bleeding and chronic exhaustion,
the medical playbook dictates the same routine. Prescribe a cream,
write a script for anxiety and send them home.
But while cancer rates are falling in seniors, they’re surging in young adults.
This forces treatable, early stage malignancies into stage 4 death warrants.
People are being failed by the healthcare system… and it’s terminal.
Every year, cancer claims the lives of 626,000 Americans.
But it isn’t actually one disease. It’s a silent mutator that crowds out the body’s healthy cells.
We all think we know the signs.
Skin cancer is easy to spot. Breast cancer has extensive awareness.
Prostate cancer is caught by regular screening. And lung cancer heavily targets obvious risk
factors like smoking. But there’s one common killer hiding in plain sight.
And the numbers are exploding.
Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer death in young adults.
In 2026 alone, there are expected to be over 158,000 cases diagnosed.
Around 55,000 will die.
Caught early enough, and it has a near perfect survival rate. Caught late… and it’s just a
matter of time. Yet, 3 out of 4 young adults are being given a terminal diagnosis. Why?
Part of the reason is the symptoms center entirely around the bathroom.
Patients are too embarrassed to talk about it. Doctors are too quick to dismiss it.
Unwarranted shame is killing people.
The system is actually working for seniors. In the most recent study,
it was shown that the rate of colorectal cancer among older patients had dropped by 2.5%.
Routine screenings are prescribed for anyone over age 45, and they act like early warning systems.
Doctors are able to monitor any risk factors early. Noncancerous polyps are often found early,
long before they can develop into cancer, and removed via minimally invasive surgeries.
But it’s not all down to healthcare professionals.
Seniors are getting healthier. Part of this is the improvement in elder care,
but the other element is how much healthier everyone is living. The rates of smoking
have dropped massively, partially due to anti-smoking campaigns and taxes.
The access to better, reasonably priced food means the heavily processed diets of the past
are being phased out. Better digestive health means a lower rate of cancer.
But on the other end of the spectrum, something disturbing is happening.
As much as they don’t want to admit it, millennials are slouching towards middle age.
The oldest millennials have crossed the age 45 threshold, which is where the recommendation for
colonoscopy screenings begins. But even among the younger millennials and Gen Z,
doctors are watching nervously as the rate of colorectal cancer ticks up. At last count,
it was rising about 3% per year among adults ages 20 to 49. Even the younger
Gen Z are getting a rude awakening that their own body can turn on them at any time.
And it’s not just one kind of cancer.
The rate of colorectal cancer is the most stark, but doctors have seen an
increased risk of breast cancer, skin cancer, and cervical cancer in young people. But for most,
it's a background threat. Something that most young people simply don’t want to think about.
In some cases, the risk is genetic. This is especially common in breast cancer,
where women are tested early for the BRCA gene. Up to 10% of cancers are caused by a genetic risk,
but that still leaves the remaining 90%. And those are caused by outside factors or bad luck.
For millennials and Gen Z, this might come as a shock to them. After all,
they pride themselves on being healthier than past generations.
But the world may not be going along with that.
Among the biggest risk factors that have been removed for these younger generations,
smoking and drinking stand out. The rate of smoking is only 11% of young adults,
including millennials and Gen Z. And while the majority of younger adults drink alcohol,
the percentage of heavy drinkers is much lower than in Gen Z and Baby Boomers.
But those same healthy habits may be backfiring on them.
Colorectal, pancreatic, and kidney cancer are all linked to excess weight. But these three cancers
don’t explain the full increase. Another major factor might be those snacks itself,
as processed foods, nitrates, and saturated fats have been linked to an increase in breast,
prostate, and colon cancer. The latter in particular is a high risk.
The digestive system is being put through its paces by the average American diet,
and unlike with smoking, the damage caused by it isn’t noticeable until it might be too late.
Many Millennials and Gen Z are walking around with a ticking time bomb inside.
Behavior also plays a role.
Around 66% of Gen Z describes themselves as physically active,
but that’s far lower than past generations. People are still living sedentary lifestyles.
While lack of physical activity isn’t a cancer risk directly,
it does mean people don’t get the benefits of working out. That helps reduce inflammation in
the body and regulates hormone levels. Up to 15 types of cancer may have their risk level
decreased by physical activity, and that’s something this generation is missing out on.
Slowly but surely, it’s all adding up.
Adults born around 1990 are between 2 and 3 times more likely to develop more aggressive,
rare malignancies like pancreatic, kidney, and small intestine cancers. These don’t directly
track with family history. Instead, they are linked to metabolic shifts driven by
modern lifestyles. There’s an entire generation that’s increasingly comfortable staying at home,
being sedentary and missing out on physical activity.
The lack of movement increases the conditions that cancer thrives in.
This comfort zone is causing a fatal delay.
Young people are hesitant to leave the house for routine doctor appointments or early screenings.
It’s a trend that doctors are becoming increasingly concerned about. As health
for seniors gets better, health for young people is getting worse. This means the baseline risk
trajectory is moving in the exact opposite direction it was supposed to. A system set
up for more healthcare for seniors and less for young people is exposing a serious vulnerability.
And it isn’t equipped for what comes next.
Cancer is typically considered a disease of aging, the lifetime of cellular damage.
Our bodies eventually lose the ability to repair malformed cells,
allowing them to mutate into tumors and shut down organs. Because of this,
doctors have spent decades to be on the lookout for signs of damage in older people.
But now that medical timeline has been shattered.
It’s not just that young people are getting cancer faster than expected. On a cellular level,
they’re literally aging faster. A major study by researchers at
Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis confirmed the generational shift.
Younger people are in fact aging faster than older generations… but not in the way people think.
But that doesn’t mean the damage isn’t accumulating inside.
One of the biggest cancer risks scientists look for is the gap between biological age
and chronological age. The latter is how long we’ve been alive, the former is how
old our bodies appear to be. The factors that can create that divergence include obesity,
sedentary behavior, poor diet, alcohol consumption, and issues with the metabolism.
Surprisingly, there is some correlation between being born by cesarean section
and these risk factors. However, each of these individual factors is considered to be minor.
But when you combine them all, you get a big problem.
A study analyzed data from 150,000 young adults in the United Kingdom,
and combined it with 10,000 individuals in the US as part of a larger database.
They used 9 blood biochemistry markers linked with critical organs that can
develop cancer to create a map of how fast our bodies are decaying from the inside out.
What they discovered was a nightmare for millennials and Gen Z.
The shift has been accelerating for decades. Gen X was already
aging slightly faster than Baby Boomers. It was a slight change,
but it was the start of a dark pattern. Those born between 1990 and 1999 displayed systemic
aging that was 92% higher when pitted against the generations before them.
And the faster you age, the faster the risk.
This study showed that the younger group had an 8% risk increase for early-onset cancers. For those
who had the most advanced aging factors, those results surged to a 15% increase. Scientists have
been raising the alarm to let young people know that something is increasing their risk of cancer.
17 of 34 major cancer types show an increased risk among Millennials and Gen X. And Gen Z is likely
to follow. They hope the awareness will lead to more young people getting early screenings.
Word of this increased cancer risk has been slow to spread,
but it is spreading. Millennials have been grudgingly admitting
that they’re getting older and taking the necessary steps to safeguard their health.
But is it too late?
As for Gen Z, the younger generation has been criticized for oversharing, but that’s led to many
being very open with their health struggles. News articles have talked about their openness with
taboo topics like gastrointestinal issues, with sufferers starting online support groups. That
allows peers to sometimes identify when something isn’t just an annoyance - it’s a warning sign.
But can they get anyone to take it seriously?
There are often a lot of roadblocks in the way of young people getting checked for cancer risks.
First, specialists can have a lengthy waiting list, and the list is even longer if you’re
trying to go outside of work hours. Specialized tests are expensive, and if the patient is under
the age of recommended testing and doesn’t have a referral, it may not be covered by insurance.
With many younger workers stuck in freelance gig work, they’re stuck paying out of pocket
and may be forced to resort to convincing a general practitioner that they need a referral.
There’s a new term on everyone’s lips when it comes to this new risk factor:
“Medical Gaslighting”.
Historically, this kind of institutional neglect heavily targeted women. A female patient would
describe specific pain, only for a doctor to shrug it off as “stress” or “cycle issues”,
prescribe an aspirin and move on. Countless women were stuck with
painful or even fatal conditions because the doctor refused to look a little deeper.
Things have changed.
But it might have spread to an entire generation.
Gaslighting isn’t just a toxic relationship trait where someone tries to convince you that you’re
crazy. In the healthcare industry, it’s a deadly form of manipulation.
It’s used to convince patients that they’re hallucinating their physical suffering.
Of course, doctors aren’t supposed to cause harm, aren’t they?
In some cases, it’s simply trying to get through a busy schedule of patients without having to
try to squeeze in hard-to-schedule tests. But the consequences of that delay and diversion
can be worsening quality of life, or in the case of cancer, even an early death.
And more young people are starting to stand up to it.
Especially when it comes to new and hard-to-diagnose ailments, doctors tend
to fall back on the textbook Most of the time, the most likely solution will be the correct one.
But for those who come in with the less-likely outcome, that’s cold comfort as their health
continues to deteriorate. So after dealing with too many dead ends as they tried to get diagnosed,
young people are starting to take charge of their own medical appointments and come prepared.
And it takes some doctors by surprise.
Instead of coming in and letting the doctor take the lead, Gen Z in particular has been
entering appointments like they know what they want and they won’t take no for an answer.
They’ll come with journals of their symptoms, questions for the doctor, and even sometimes a
friend to act as a witness. This has been spurred on by increased coverage of medical gaslighting,
and those who are in the know come ready to fend it off at the first sign.
This is one of the few bright sides of the increase in dangerous illnesses among the young:
those who know about it are incentivized to take charge of their health.
At this point, there’s no doubt left. Something is wrong with the young health-wise. While
the elderly are benefiting from better overall health care and seeing their cancer rates drop,
the young are seeing it skyrocket without a clear pattern. It can’t simply be blamed on
behavior and individual health. It’s happening too fast and among different kinds of cancer.
Is there something larger at play here?
If so, is it too late to stop it?
There have been plenty of theories about the cause of the surge in cancer and other “older” illnesses
among millennials and Gen Z. Some, like both vaccines and the aftereffects of Covid-19, have
been heavily debunked, and this pattern was going on well before the 2020 crisis. But what’s been
going on as well during that period is the surge in pollution and the advance in climate change.
The Earth is changing, and it seems to be becoming a harder place to live in for many people.
And many young people feel that only they can protect themselves.
While this might not be the most dangerous time in human history,
the cascading crises around the world have led to a huge surge in anxiety.
But there’s something uniquely terrifying about the idea that it won’t be the world
that ends - but something in the world that puts an end to you. As word of this growing
cancer crisis spreads, Gen Z is leading the way in taking charge of their own health.
But will this be enough against a two-pronged threat?
Gen Z and millennials have been facing this crisis for a long time,
but it’s been advancing in a creeping way that makes it hard to raise the alarm. A 3% increase
in cancer rates per year doesn’t make headlines in the way that a massive plague does. After all,
people die of cancer every day, and individual cases rarely make the news. But the bigger problem
is that the health care system itself may not be set up for this crisis. For decades now,
it’s been set up to assume that young people will use less healthcare, only showing up at the
hospital in an emergency. Meanwhile the elderly take up the lion’s share of diagnostic efforts.
The medical industry isn’t prepared for this demographic shift. And it’s pushing back.
As clinics ration their time and screenings, young people are skipping the gatekeepers completely.
They’re self-diagnosing and demanding the scans and tests they need to survive.
They are fighting a disease… and the clock.
The medical world will eventually change. It’ll realize it’s on the precipice of a huge crisis.
But it's a profession that moves at a snail's pace.
There are thousands of people who don’t have that luxury.
Two generations are counting on a system that’s running out of time.
And death waits for no one.
